newsitem.title: TURKEY: Iran's Rafsanjani, Turkey want to boost trade.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Rafsanjani, Turkey want to boost trade.

text.p: Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani began a four-day visit to Turkey on Thursday designed to build on growing trade links despite U.S. efforts to isolate Tehran.
The visit marks a further step forward in strengthening ties between the two neighbouring Moslem countries since Necmettin Erbakan became Turkey's first Islamist prime minister in June.
Erbakan heralded the trip as an opportunity to build trade relations comparable with the links between France and Germany.

"Our goal is for there to be as much merchandise, people, money, planes and vehicles going between Turkey and Iran each day as between France and Germany," Erbakan told reporters ahead of talks with Rafsanjani.
He said the two countries aimed to raise trade volume to more than $2 billion in 1997 from $957 million in 1995.

The visit is likely to antagonise the United States, which is a close ally of NATO member Turkey and is trying to isolate Iran, which Washington accuses of sponsoring terrorism. Iran denies the charge.
Turkish President Suleyman Demirel defended the contacts between the two nations after talks with Rafsanjani.
"Nobody should reach false conclusions and interpretrations from the will of two neighbouring and friendly countries to work together," Demirel told reporters.
Rafsanjani was earlier met by Demirel at Ankara airport.

"Regional security, Cyprus, Iraq, the Middle East and Central Asia were among the subjects discussed," Rafsanjani said after talks with Demirel. He said there was also discussion on abolishing duties between the two countries.

A senior Turkish official told Reuters details of a preliminary study on construction of a pipeline to carry Iranian oil to Western markets through Turkey's Mediterranean terminal of Ceyhan would be discussed during the visit.
Turkey signed a $23 billion agreement for the supply of Iranian natural gas over 23 years during a visit by Erbakan to Iran in August on his first major trip abroad as prime minister.
The deal was struck days after U.S. President Bill Clinton signed a law imposing sanctions on any company investing over $40 million a year in the energy industries of Iran or Libya.
Ankara said the pipeline deal would not be affected by U.S. sanctions because Turkey was only constructing the stretch of pipeline on its own territory.
Iranian and Turkish economy officials have been meeting in Ankara this week on new agreements on trade, shipping and the foundation of a joint chamber of commerce.

Rafsanjani, who arrived with a large delegation including the foreign and oil ministers, was quoted by the Iranian news agency IRNA as saying his talks would cover the latest developments in the Gulf and Kurdish-controlled northern Iraq.
Relations between the two countries have been strained by concerns in Ankara that Kurdish rebels, seeking self-rule in southeast Turkey, have used Iran as a springboard for attacks.
